title: Widrow, Hoff, and the First Machine That Learned by Gradient Descent (1960)
explainer: In 1960, Bernard Widrow and his student Ted Hoff built ADALINE, an early trainable artificial neuron, and discovered the LMS (least-mean-squares) rule by differentiating a squared-error expression on a blackboard — in effect inventing a working, practical form of stochastic gradient descent for a real learning system, independent of and well before the term was common in machine learning. Unlike the perceptron's hard-threshold update rule, ADALINE's LMS rule adjusted weights using a continuous error signal, the same core mechanism (an estimated gradient, updated one example at a time) behind the stochastic gradient descent used to train today's networks. It's a useful corrective to thinking of gradient descent as a purely abstract tool: it was discovered by engineers wiring up analog hardware to get a machine to learn simple pattern classification.

resources.title: Thinking About Thinking: The Discovery of the LMS Algorithm
resources.source: Bernard Widrow, IEEE Signal Processing Magazine (hosted by Stanford University)
